place: Oxley is [[cast:Ebba]]'s farm in a wide, sloping meadow at the very foot of Wardlow: a low stone farmhouse with a deep hearth and a tired, low fire, a long byre that smells of hay and warm oxen, a five-barred wooden gate with an iron latch, and a brook along the bottom of the meadow with ice at its edges. The great white oxen are as gentle as old dogs and breathe out clouds of steam, and the first snow of winter comes down soft and quiet until the whole farm is white and every track shows plain. It feels humble, warm and close to the end of the road, the last kitchen before the hardest climb, with Wardlow's bare dark shoulder always above the roof and the cold beacon waiting on top.

hosts.name: Ebba
hosts.voice: Humble and plain-spoken: short sentences, farm words, no fuss, and she says exactly what she means ("Gate stays shut. That's the one rule."). Like a good host she feeds them and gives them the warm corner of the byre loft before she asks a single question, and she only asks why they are so late in the year on Friday. She talks to her oxen like old friends and calls them "my whites". She never scolds: when the gate is found open she asks plainly who opened it, worried for her oxen in the snow, not cross. Her first words to any telling are "Thank you for telling me." She has never carried fire up Wardlow, so Ember's words reach her as fox yips ("That fox wants cheese," she says, and she is right). She says only what she knows about the walking stick by her door.

hosts.name: Ned (Ebba's grandson)
hosts.voice: Loud, quick and very sure, a boy who shouts the first true thing he sees, to get someone in trouble: "It was HER, I saw!" (Ch 47), "It's her fault." (Ch 49). He loves the oxen, knows every one, and his blurting comes from worry for them, so he stays likable and is never mocked or scolded. By Ch 50 he is changing: he helps call the oxen in and says, "Sorry, [[child:youngest]]." As a child he can understand Ember. His reviewed alternate is Ted.

modeled_behavior: Tell the truth before anyone asks: "I did it. I'm sorry. How can I help?"
echo_plan: Two Odyssey shapes and one fable, all quiet. Ch 46 and 50, Eumaeus (Odyssey 14): a humble herder welcomes travelers, feeds them first and asks their errand last; reversed on Friday, when [[child:middle]] answers [[cast:Ebba]] with the plain truth, own giggle included, where Odysseus told his host tall tales. Ch 47, the cattle of the Sun (Odyssey 12): one image only, bright white cattle let loose, walking off into the snow; nobody eats, harms or is punished for them, there is no sun-god and no storm, and the oxen simply come home. Ch 48 and 50, The Honest Woodcutter (Aesop): honesty rewarded, retold without axes, gold or silver; the reward is being believed and trusted with the most important job (the salt-lick), then [[cast:Ebba]]'s oxen and cart for Wardlow. Ch 49, Marcus Aurelius (Meditations 12.17, the true thing kindly): shown only in [[child:eldest]]'s "[[child:youngest]] already told. Let's find them.", never quoted. Story text never names Homer, Aesop or the Stoics; only the Sunday plan's grown-up note may. Faith (toggle on): blessing key Ephesians 4:25 for the week, and Ch 48's own echo Proverbs 12:19 in faith_note only.

tuesday_pair.too_little: Fibbing: [[child:youngest]] says "Not me." when [[cast:Ebba]] asks who left the gate open (Ch 47). It is a wobbly tummy, not a bad heart, and nobody piles on. The middle way comes the same night: [[child:eldest]] kneels, takes [[pro:youngest.pos]] hand and asks, "Do you want to tell it yourself? I'll stand with you." In Ch 48, hand on heart, the truth is told.
tuesday_pair.too_much: Blurting (tattling, telling to get someone in trouble): [[cast:Ned]] shouts, "It was HER, I saw!" (Ch 47), and "It's her fault." again in Ch 49. The fault is unkindness, never too much truth. [[child:eldest]] doesn't blurt back: "[[child:youngest]] already told. Let's find them." Shown changing in Ch 50: [[cast:Ned]] helps call the oxen in and says, "Sorry, [[child:youngest]]."

set_piece: Calling the oxen home with the salt-lick. At breakfast, start with a teddy who left the gate open: help it put a paw on its heart and say, "I did it. I'm sorry. How can I help?", and everyone says, "Thank you for telling me." Then the oxen (grown-ups or children on hands and knees) wander off to the far side of the room, the brook-bottom. One child counts the hoofprints (spoons or paper footprints on the floor): "One, two, three, four, lots!" One child reads the tracks and leads the way. The youngest holds the salt-lick (a bowl or a folded cushion, never real salt) and calls, "Come on home!", and the oxen amble back to the byre under the table. Swap parts and play it again.
clue: Ch 50: by [[cast:Ebba]]'s door leans a plain walking stick. "An old woman left it last winter," [[cast:Ebba]] says, and that is all she knows. After Ch 45 the children can guess whose it is, and they look at each other; nobody names [[cast:Hild]], and nobody explains it. It points ahead to Ch 55, when [[cast:Hild]] rides up Wardlow on [[cast:Ebba]]'s wood-cart.
friday_question: Why do you think [[cast:Ebba]] trusted [[child:youngest]] more after [[block:fq10.a]] told the truth?

trial.title: The Open Gate

bands.3-4: Say "I did it" about one small thing this week (a spill, a drop, a toy left out), with a hand on your heart if you like. Everyone says "Thank you for telling me."
bands.5-6: Tell what really happened in a squabble, both sides, your part too.
bands.7-9: Tell a grown-up something true before being asked: something you did, forgot or broke, big or small, and own your part.

trial.play_it_version: No spill or squabble this week? Play it with toys. Teddy leaves the toy-farm gate open and the cows wander off: help Teddy put a paw on its heart and say, "I did it. I'm sorry. How can I help?" Everyone says, "Thank you for telling me," and Teddy helps call the cows home. Two toys squabble over one block: tell what really happened, both sides. A played trial stamps the map too.
trial.safety_line: Grown-ups: say "Thank you for telling me" first, every time, before anything else, and keep any fixing small and kind, so telling stays safe. For the toy version, use toys too big to swallow.

i_can.Little: I can say "I did it" when something spills or breaks.
i_can.Middle: I can tell what really happened, my part too, even if I might get in trouble.
i_can.Big: I can tell the truth before anyone asks, and own my part.
i_can.Stretch: I can tell a hard truth kindly, and I won't go along with a fib.

in_real_life: In real life, we only go into someone's house with our grown-up.
In real life, only grown-ups carry a flame.
In real life, we tell our grown-ups about every new friend, and a good friend never asks us to keep a secret from them.
In real life, we never open a gate or a door without our grown-up's yes, and we only go near big animals with our grown-up beside us.
In real life, if an animal gets lost, we tell a grown-up and look together, and we never step onto ice.
flags_for_jon: No Part 9 sheet at drafting time (parts drafted in parallel), so continuity came from the canon's Part 9 rows; it has now been checked against the Part 9 sheet. Ch 46 opens with Grandma's reply to the Ch 45 letter, then "Last time…" carrying Part 9's Keepers' Stones trial as a story memory. The Ch 45 letter was sent from the keepers' shelter with Hild by the door, which the Part 9 sheet counts as a roof with a host under the letter rule (please confirm). Hild is absent all of Part 10, so Ch 46 needs one line on how they parted at Stanbury (proposed: she and Dun see them off from the shelter door and follow at Dun's pace). She must reach Oxley by the longest night to ride up on Ebba's cart in Ch 55; proposed, she arrives at the farm that afternoon, after the children have set off.

Timeline, set in the continuity pass (the Part 9 and Part 11 sheets agree; please confirm). Ch 45 is "six nights before the longest night". The walk from Stanbury to Oxley takes the two days between Ch 45 and Ch 46, off the page (Wardlow is "far off" from Stanbury), with the children housed at farm doors on the Keepers' Way by its old law. Part 10 then covers three story days: Ch 46 is day three; Ch 47 and 48 are day four (Ch 48 "opens with the telling", straight after Ch 47); Ch 49 and 50 are day five; Ember takes the Ch 50 letter that night and is back before dawn, and Ch 51 sets off on day six, the longest night. The drafts count nights in words only where needed, never a date. (Part 11's sheet had assumed five nights at Oxley; it now follows this count.)

Canon tension about the stick. Canon section 1 has Hild carry a plain walking stick in every scene, yet the Ch 50 clue says her stick has leaned by Ebba's door since last winter. The canon wins, so Ch 50 says only "a plain walking stick: an old woman left it last winter." Proposed reading, for your OK: it is the "one stick" Dame Blythe saw her carry west (Ch 20), beacon wood she leaned on and never got to lay; Ebba's cart brought her down, and the stick stayed. Continuity pass: the Part 11 sheet now pays it off the same way: Ebba brings it up on the cart and hands it to Hild in one line, and when the children ask her to lay the last stick, it is that one.

Ebba can't understand Ember, because Edith's list in Ch 40 is only Grandma, Edith and Hild. So she hears yips, and the talking-friend "In real life" line is needed. Ned is a child, and by canon section 1 only children understand Ember, so he can. The drafts should use this lightly, and it needs a check against Part 11 and Ch 56.

Safety against canon. Clara opening the gate (Ch 47) is the canon's mistake, but it matches two CORE_RULES tests: opening a door without a grown-up's yes, and contact with big animals. "In real life" line 4 covers both. Proposed detail inside the beat: Clara opens the gate a little to pat the calf's nose from outside the field, the calf trots out to her and stays by her, she never goes in among the oxen, Hugh is a few steps away, and the oxen amble out slowly. Ebba's question is plain, not cross.

Vote 10's option B, "along the frozen brook": everyone stays on the bank and never steps onto the ice, and the oxen stand in the brook-bottom meadow, not in the water. Proposed: Ebba walks with them on the Ch 49 search, because it is snowy hills at dusk, while the children make every choice (reading tracks, counting, calling). This needs "In real life" line 5 and a chair version of the brook bank (bible section 6).

One-child families. Bible section 6 gives sibling beats to Ned in Part 10, but Ned is the blurter in Ch 47 to 49. Proposed: "I'll stand with you" (Ch 47 and 48) and "Already told. Let's find them." (Ch 49) go to Ember, and Ned takes sibling beats only from his sorry in Ch 50 (and in Ch 56). Ned's alternate is Ted. Ebba has no reviewed alternate yet (production step 6).

Turn child: the eldest (order Hugh, Clara, Alfie per bible section 5, itself flagged). The Big default plan ("If I did something nobody saw, then I tell before anyone asks…") has no natural moment in Ch 49 as written. Proposed detail that leaves the beat alone: Hugh reads one track wrong and says so before anyone notices ("I read that wrong. Let's go back."). The knots are never brought up.

Modeled behavior, "before anyone asks": Clara is asked in Ch 47 and says "Not me." In Ch 48 she goes to Ebba herself, before being asked again. The canon line "I did it. I'm sorry. How can I help?" is hers, and Ebba's answer to "How can I help?" is the salt-lick. Alfie tells his giggle in Ch 50 before anyone asks. The line is nine words, over the eight-word Should for a 3-year-old, but canon wording is exempt. The Friday question touches the youngest's mistake, so the youngest never answers first. Its [[block:fq10.a]] is "she" by default, with he and they versions ("told" doesn't change).

Alfie's job is the night latch, and the gate is opened in daylight, so no blame reaches Alfie. Ch 48's "remember when" (from Ch 19) is suggested as Clara's own moment waking the boys, placed after her telling, so Ember hands back a memory and never the answer. Hild is absent, and canon section 1 says that by Part 10 the children ask each other Hild's questions. Hugh's "Do you want to tell it yourself?" is the model: he asks, and he never tells Clara what to do.

Proposed details with no new names: seven white oxen and one white calf (Alfie counts; Ember manages "four, lots"). Ebba's ox-call is "Come on home, come on home!", and Clara's version is "Come on home!". The oxen stay unnamed, so no name check is needed.

"In real life": five lines, about 100 words, is too long for the dinner card (kit 13.1). Suggested: the Sunday plan carries lines 1 to 3, which other parts share, and the dinner card carries lines 4 and 5, which are new to Part 10 and go beyond bible section 5's four motifs (a production call, like kit open item 20). Continuity pass: the friend line now reads "a good friend" in every part (Part 1's wording, which also avoids "real" twice in one sentence).

Kit against strengths: kit 9a's Truth-Teller note leaves out the first sentence of strengths' proposed Part 10 Sunday-plan note ("This week's too-much side includes tattling: telling to get someone in trouble."). Strengths ranks above the kit, so Part 10 should print the full strengths wording.

Trial: each band starts with the canon's task word for word, with small additions. There is a play-it version because the Little and Middle tasks need a real spill or squabble. The safety line comes from strengths' "grown-up's half" ("Thank you for telling me" first), plus a small-toy line. Faith: the blessing key Ephesians 4:25 still carries strengths flag 4 (shortened). Ch 48 uses its own canon verse, Proverbs 12:19 ESV.

Week words "trust" and "wander" are both everyday words, and no other part sends either home. The repeats this sheet found at drafting time are fixed: Part 1 now has "flicker" (Part 3 keeps "courteous") and Part 6 now has "cling" (Part 2 keeps "peer"). "Honest" was left out on purpose, because "honest girl" would be praise of who a child is; Part 11 had picked it and now uses "admit".
